EXECUTIVE MEMORANDUM: ANALYSIS OF INVESTOR MARKUP
CONVERTIBLE NOTE PURCHASE AGREEMENT REVIEW
Eve Litigation LLP – Emerging Companies & Venture Capital Practice

TO:       Board of Directors & Finance Committee
FROM:     Legal Counsel
RE:       Investor Markup Review – Convertible Note Purchase Agreement
DATE:     Current
MATTER:   Emerging Companies Venture Capital – Bridge Loan/Convertible Note Financing

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum analyzes the investor's markup to our convertible note purchase agreement in light of the board-approved term sheet. Our review identifies material deviations, areas of acceptable market practice, and provisions requiring board attention before execution.

Key findings:
• Three provisions deviate materially from board-approved terms
• Five provisions fall within market-standard ranges for emerging company financings
• Two provisions contain favorable modifications to our benefit
• Recommended path forward includes targeted counter-proposals on identified deviations

DETAILED ANALYSIS

1. CONVERSION MECHANICS & VALUATION CAP

Board-Approved Term: Conversion on Series A priced round at pre-agreed $[X] million post-money valuation cap.

Investor Markup: Markup introduces dual-trigger conversion mechanism with optional investor election at six-month anniversary, AND introduces floating valuation cap indexed to subsequent Series A pricing.

Analysis:
• The optional election feature creates uncertainty regarding conversion timing and dilution profile
• Floating valuation cap shifts downside protection risk entirely to Company
• Market practice: Fixed caps are standard; optional election provisions are uncommon in bridge conversions
• Risk to Company: Investor optionality may delay Series A close or depress valuations

Recommendation: Counter-propose maintaining fixed valuation cap with time-certain (non-optional) conversion trigger at Series A close or specified date (e.g., 18-month anniversary), whichever is earlier.

2. INTEREST RATE & ACCRUAL MECHANICS

Board-Approved Term: [X]% annual simple interest, paid upon conversion/maturity.

Investor Markup: Increases to [X+1.5]% with compound accrual semi-annually and mandatory payment in cash prior to conversion.

Analysis:
• Rate increase materially increases cost of capital
• Compound accrual vs. simple interest compounds effective yield
• Mandatory cash payment obligation may stress near-term liquidity if not carefully timed
• Market practice: Simple interest paid at conversion is more favorable to borrowers; mandatory pre-conversion cash payments are less common in bridge notes
• Impact: Additional [Y] basis points of annual cost over bridge period

Recommendation: Counter at [X+0.75]% with simple annual interest accruing but deferred to maturity/conversion (standard market). If investor requires current cash servicing, propose tiered rate: [X]% if deferred, [X+1]% if paid currently.

3. REPRESENTATIONS & WARRANTIES

Board-Approved Term: Standard corporate, capitalization, and litigation reps; 18-month survival period post-conversion.

Investor Markup: Expanded reps regarding competitive positioning, customer concentration, technology IP ownership, regulatory compliance (including anticipated environmental permits); survival extended to 24 months.

Analysis:
• IP ownership representation is appropriate for tech-focused deals (standard market)
• Competitive positioning and customer concentration reps are commercially sensitive and less common in bridge instruments
• Environmental permit rep may impose disproportionate burden if regulatory landscape is evolving
• 24-month survival is longer than standard (typically 12–18 months for bridge conversions)
• Risk: Expanded reps increase indemnification exposure post-funding and may reveal competitive information to investor

Recommendation: Accept IP ownership, regulatory compliance (as currently anticipated), and capitalization reps as standard. Counter on competitive positioning rep (market sensitivity). Propose 18-month cap on survival or carve-out for environmental permits pending formal guidance. Clarify indemnification basket, caps, and escrow mechanics if reps are materially breached.

4. INFORMATION RIGHTS & GOVERNANCE

Board-Approved Term: Quarterly financial statements and annual audit; no board seat.

Investor Markup: Monthly unaudited financials, quarterly audited financials, annual strategic plan submission, quarterly governance call with investor participation, and right to designate observer to board meetings (non-voting).

Analysis:
• Monthly reporting is operationally burdensome for early-stage companies but increasingly standard in bridge rounds
• Observer rights (non-voting) are market-standard for investors and not problematic if properly scoped
• Governance calls are reasonable
• Strategic plan submission may raise confidentiality concerns if investor has competitive relationships
• Impact: Administrative overhead; potential disclosure of strategic vulnerabilities

Recommendation: Accept quarterly (audited) and monthly (unaudited) reporting as market standard. Accept observer rights. Counter on strategic plan submission by proposing high-level roadmap only, with carve-outs for confidential competitive strategy. Confirm observer attendance parameters and confidentiality obligations.

5. ANTI-DILUTION & ADJUSTMENT MECHANICS

Board-Approved Term: Broad-based weighted average anti-dilution adjustments; conversion price cap subject to [X]% floor.

Investor Markup: Narrows to narrow-based weighted average; eliminates price floor; introduces "pay-to-play" mechanism requiring bridge note holder to participate pro-rata in down round or face conversion price increase.

Analysis:
• Narrow-based weighted average is more investor-favorable but still within market range
• Elimination of price floor removes upside protection from Company equity holders
• Pay-to-play mechanic is market-standard in institutional rounds but uncommon in bridges
• Pay-to-play creates economic pressure on investors to fund subsequent rounds (potentially positive) but shifts risk to non-participating investors
• Risk: If subsequent Series dilutes significantly, Company equity holders bear adjustment burden; pay-to-play may foreclose options if Company opts out of down round

Recommendation: Propose reversion to broad-based weighted average (current preference in early-stage markets). If investor insists on narrow-based, propose reinstatement of 90% price floor and clarify that pay-to-play mechanic applies only to explicitly subsequent priced rounds (not bridges or SAFE instruments). Include carve-out: investors in current bridge note are excluded from pay-to-play if bridge note is converted before pay-to-play trigger event.

6. MATURITY & DEFAULT PROVISIONS

Board-Approved Term: [X]-year maturity from funding; events of default limited to non-payment and material covenant breach (with cure periods).

Investor Markup: Maturity extended to [X+1] years; events of default expanded to include: change of control without investor consent, material adverse business change, failure to achieve operational milestones, debt covenant breaches with 3rd parties, and unilateral investor termination right if Company valuation falls below [Y]% of pre-money valuation at funding.

Analysis:
• Extended maturity is acceptable (one additional year is manageable)
• Change-of-control consent requirement is problematic and non-standard for bridge notes—creates potential deadlock in M&A scenarios
• Material adverse business change ("MAC") is vague and subjective; triggers protracted disputes
• Operational milestone tying (e.g., revenue targets) is more appropriate for performance-based instruments, not bridges
• Valuation-based unilateral termination is unusual for debt and creates adverse incentive: investor incentivized to downvalue company to trigger put right
• Risk: Excessive defaults and investor put options may constrain strategic flexibility and create funding uncertainty

Recommendation: Accept maturity extension to [X+1] years. Counter as follows:
  – Change of control: Propose carve-out permitting change of control with investor notice (not consent); investor retains repayment priority at close.
  – MAC clause: Replace with defined list of specific triggering events (e.g., loss of [X]% of revenue contracts, key executive departure). Require good faith determination with dispute resolution mechanism.
  – Operational milestones: Delete entirely; milestones are not appropriate for convertible instruments.
  – Valuation termination right: Delete. Propose alternative: if Series A does not close by [date], investor may elect conversion at fixed cap or redemption at par (not at discount).

7. REDEMPTION & PUT RIGHTS

Board-Approved Term: No redemption prior to maturity; upon maturity, Company may elect conversion or repayment.

Investor Markup: Introduces unilateral investor redemption right (put) upon maturity at 1.25x principal plus accrued interest; Company obligated to pay within 60 days.

Analysis:
• Put right is investor-favorable and creates repayment obligation (debt characteristic) rather than conversion optionality
• 1.25x multiplier is reasonable return for bridge financing
• 60-day payment window may be operationally challenging if Series A has not closed
• Risk: Creates hard liquidity requirement at maturity; if Series A is delayed, Company must fund redemption from operations or draw on credit facilities

Recommendation: Accept put right structure as market-standard but counter on terms: (1) Extend payment window to 120 days to align with typical post-Series A closing timeline; (2) Clarify that put right does not apply if Series A conversion has occurred; (3) Propose carve-out: if Company is actively fundraising (evidenced by board resolution), put right may be extended by mutual consent up to 6 months (with minimal interest accrual during extension).

8. INVESTMENT MECHANICS & CLOSING CONDITIONS

Board-Approved Term: Standard representations, capitalization schedule, corporate documents, material agreements, and third-party consents.

Investor Markup: Adds conditions: (1) Audited financial statements prepared by Big Four firm, (2) Third-party solvency opinion, (3) Insurance certificate naming investor as loss payee, (4) Technology IP audit by independent counsel, (5) Compliance certificate regarding export controls and sanctions, (6) No material adverse change since signing.

Analysis:
• Audited financials by Big Four is operationally expensive and potentially disruptive for early-stage companies
• Solvency opinion is unusual for bridge notes and suggests investor concern about capital structure
• Insurance and IP audit conditions are reasonable but increase closing costs
• Export/sanctions compliance is appropriate given regulatory environment
• MAC condition at closing is standard but should be defined narrowly

Recommendation: Counter on Big Four audited financials—propose SSARS review or audit by qualified independent CPA (not necessarily Big Four) with investor right to select provider. Accept solvency opinion (standard in institutional rounds). Accept insurance naming, IP audit, and compliance certificate as reasonable. Propose MAC condition limited to defined triggering events (not subjective).

9. GOVERNANCE & AMENDMENT PROVISIONS

Board-Approved Term: Amendments require written consent of Company and investors representing 50% of principal.

Investor Markup: Amendments require unanimity (100% investor consent); adds drag-along rights allowing holders of 66.67% of principal to force conversion or redemption; adds information rights amendments requiring investor consent even to eliminate/modify.

Analysis:
• Unanimity requirement is more restrictive than market-standard (typically 50–75%)
• Drag-along at 66.67% is reasonable control threshold (less than majority)
• Locking amendments in information rights reduces Company operational flexibility
• Risk: Difficult to obtain amendments if multiple bridge investors with misaligned interests

Recommendation: Propose amendment threshold of 75% (supermajority, market-standard for convertible instruments with multiple investors). Accept drag-along at 66.67%. Carve out operational amendments (e.g., payment details, reporting formats) from consent requirements.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED COUNTER-PROPOSALS

Priority 1 (Material Deviations – Require Resolution):
1. Conversion mechanics: Fix valuation cap, remove optional election
2. Interest rate: Reduce to [X+0.75]% with simple accrual and deferred payment
3. Default provisions: Narrow events of default, remove valuation-based put, delete operational milestones
4. Change of control: Modify to notice-only with repayment priority

Priority 2 (Market-Standard – Consider Acceptance):
5. Representations expansion: Accept IP/compliance reps; limit competitive positioning; cap survival at 18 months
6. Information rights: Accept monthly/quarterly reporting and observer rights; limit strategic plan scope
7. Anti-dilution: Accept narrow-based weighted average with 90% price floor; clarify pay-to-play scope

Priority 3 (Operational Accommodations – Negotiate Terms):
8. Closing conditions: Replace Big Four audit requirement; accept IP audit and compliance certificate
9. Redemption put: Accept structure; extend payment window to 120 days; add conversion carve-out
10. Amendment threshold: Propose 75% supermajority; carve out operational amendments

LEGAL CONSIDERATIONS & MARKET CONTEXT

This convertible note financing is structured appropriately for bridge capital in the emerging companies space. However, the investor's markup introduces several provisions that shift risk disproportionately toward the Company:

• Optionality mechanics (conversion timing, investor redemption) create uncertainty in financial planning
• Subjective default triggers (MAC, competitive positioning) increase litigation risk
• Expanded representations extend indemnification exposure post-conversion
• Liquidity requirements (cash interest, put redemption) stress near-term cash flow

The recommended counter-proposals balance investor protections with operational flexibility and align with current market practice for Series A-stage bridge conversions in the emerging companies space.

CONCLUSION & NEXT STEPS

1. Present recommended counter-proposals to investor (Priorities 1 & 2)
2. Prepare fallback positions on Priority 3 items for negotiation
3. If investor resists key Priority 1 items, escalate to Board for risk tolerance assessment
4. Once agreed, prepare final execution copy with integration of all agreed changes
5. Implement investor information rights; establish governance calendar

This analysis reflects current market practice and our firm's experience in emerging companies venture capital financings. We recommend Board review and approval of the counter-proposal strategy before formal submission to investor.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
